extracted.intended_audience: registered patent attorneys and USPTO adjudicators (respondents in reciprocal discipline matters)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules the USPTO Director applies when deciding whether to impose reciprocal discipline based on a state's ethical suspension or disbarment, including the respondent's burdens to show due process defects, infirmity of proof, or grave injustice. Also covers post-suspension administrative duties and appeal timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal-discipline presumption and directive (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall consider any timely filed response and shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact that one of the listed defenses applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation text quoted and applied: the default presumption is to impose identical discipline; the listed defenses (due process deprivation, infirmity of proof, grave injustice, or that the practitioner was not publicly disciplined) are the exclusive grounds to avoid identical discipline. Examples: Director imposed three-year suspension identical to Illinois suspension because respondent did not meet the heavy proof requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent's burden and standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent reciprocal discipline the practitioner must demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, a genuine issue of material fact as to one of the § 11.24(d)(1) defenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts and the USPTO apply a narrow standard — the respondent bears the burden and must meet the clear-and-convincing evidentiary standard. Cited cases: In re Kramer, In re Friedman, Selling v. Radford; respondent must do more than disagreement with state findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due-process deprivation criterion (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: The procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process requires 'the opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner.' (Mathews v. Eldridge). In disciplinary proceedings, due process is satisfied where respondent had reasonable notice, attended and participated, could present evidence, testify, cross-examine, and present argument. Challenges to substantive discovery rulings (e.g., striking experts, limiting subpoenas/interrogatories) ordinarily do not constitute deprivation of due process absent evidence that meaningful participation was denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity-of-proof criterion (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: There was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The showing is difficult — respondent must do more than challenge the factfinder's weighing of evidence or assert errors in discovery; must show specific evidence that undermines the state finding. Deference is generally given to state factfinders (see In re Zdravkovich). Failure to identify what omitted evidence would have changed the result is fatal to this defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave-injustice criterion (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: The imposition of the same public censure/reprimand/probation/disbarment/suspension/disciplinary disqualification by the Office would result in a grave injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis focuses on whether the severity of the punishment 'fits' the misconduct and permits consideration of mitigating factors and precedent. Courts inquire whether the state-imposed sanction was so ill-fitted to the adjudicated misconduct that reciprocal discipline would be a grave injustice. Showing must be by clear and convincing evidence and typically requires demonstrating the state sanction was outside the appropriate range or was based on extraordinary circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument that practitioner was not publicly disciplined (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified can be asserted to prevent imposition of reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicitly enumerated ground in the regulation: if the state action was not a public discipline of the listed kinds, that fact can prevent imposition of identical discipline by the USPTO. The practitioner must show a genuine issue of material fact on this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director's limited-review/deference principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director (like a federal court) is not sitting as a court of review to discover errors in the state courts' proceedings and gives deference to state determinations of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority (Selling; In re Zdravkovich; In re Sibley): review is narrow; federal (or USPTO) review asks only whether Selling elements are met. Disagreement with outcome or reweighing evidence is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability (and limits) of statutory and constitutional defenses (e.g., 47 U.S.C. § 230, First Amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes and constitutional protections may be raised, but their applicability depends on the nature of the conduct: for example, CDA § 230 protects interactive computer services for third-party content, not an author of his own allegedly false statements; knowingly false or reckless falsehoods are not protected by the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent cannot invoke Section 230 to immunize her own statements on a weblog; Alvarez and Garrison explain that knowing or reckless falsehoods lack First Amendment protection. Practitioners should show how a statute or constitutional case law specifically negates the disciplinary finding, not merely cite statutes unrelated to the misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-order publication and notification duties (37 C.F.R. § 11.59 and related)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reciprocal discipline is imposed, the OED Director shall publish notice (e.g., in the Official Gazette) and give notice of the public discipline and reasons to disciplinary agencies in states where respondent is admitted, courts of admission, and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final Order directs OED Director to make public Notice in the Official Gazette and to provide notice pursuant to § 11.59 to state disciplinary agencies, courts, and the public; disciplinary decisions available in OED FOIA Reading Room. This is an administrative requirement following imposition of discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative and operational consequences of suspension (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.57; USPTO internal actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent must comply with duties enumerated in § 11.58; the USPTO will dissociate respondent's name from any Customer Numbers and PKI certificates; respondent shall not apply for or obtain a USPTO Customer Number nor have her name added to one until reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical operational effects include dissociation from Customer Numbers, revocation/association removal of public key infrastructure (PKI) certificates, and categorical prohibition on obtaining or being added to customer numbers until reinstatement to practice before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review and timing for petition (35 U.S.C. § 32; E.D. Va. rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review of the final decision by the USPTO Director may be had by a Petition filed with the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia under 35 U.S.C. § 32 within thirty (30) days after the date of the order recording the Director's action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must file within the 30-day window; local rules (e.g., E.D.Va. Local Civil Rule 83.5) apply. This is the exclusive federal judicial avenue referenced for review of USPTO disciplinary orders.
